notes: Short source chapter — 6 Objective I items, all rebuilt, topped up to 10 with items on the spectrum, energy density and radiation pressure. Worked examples number 8; the source's own worked set is brief.

practice_bank.title: Practice — Electromagnetic Waves
practice_bank.intro: Ten questions on electromagnetic waves. The unifying idea: a changing electric field makes a magnetic field and vice versa, so the two sustain each other through empty space.

sections.title: What Makes an Electromagnetic Wave
sections.blurb: Maxwell's missing term, and what radiates.

items.prompt: A magnetic field can be produced by
options: both a moving charge and a changing electric field
items.explanation: Conduction current (moving charge) and displacement current (a changing electric field) both source a magnetic field. Maxwell's addition of the second term to Ampere's law was what made electromagnetic waves possible — without it the theory is inconsistent for a charging capacitor.

items.prompt: A compass needle sits in the gap of a parallel-plate capacitor that is being charged through a resistor. The needle
options: deflects while the capacitor charges and returns as the charging current dies away
deflects and stays deflected as long as the battery is connected
deflects only at the instant the circuit is broken
items.explanation: While charging, the electric field between the plates is changing, so a displacement current flows there and produces a magnetic field. Once the capacitor is fully charged the field stops changing, the displacement current ceases, and the needle returns — over a time set by the circuit's $ RC $ constant.

options: a charge moving at constant velocity
items.explanation: A static charge has only a steady electric field; one moving uniformly adds a steady magnetic field. Only *acceleration* makes the fields change in the self-sustaining way that detaches them as radiation. This is why antennas drive charges back and forth, and why circular accelerators lose energy as synchrotron radiation.

Since $ c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0} $, the quantity $ 1/\mu_0\varepsilon_0 $ equals $ c^{2} $ and has the dimensions of a velocity squared. Maxwell's realisation that this combination of two purely electrical constants gave the measured speed of light was the moment optics became part of electromagnetism.

sections.title: Structure of the Wave
sections.blurb: E, B and the direction of travel — mutually perpendicular, in fixed ratio.

items.prompt: For an electromagnetic wave in vacuum described by $ E = E_0\sin(kx - \omega t) $ and $ B = B_0\sin(kx - \omega t) $,
items.explanation: The field amplitudes are locked in the ratio $ E_0/B_0 = c $, and for any wave $ c = \omega/k $. Combining gives $ E_0/B_0 = \omega/k $, i.e. $ E_0 k = B_0\omega $. The two fields peak together and vanish together — they are in phase, not a quarter cycle apart.

items.prompt: In an electromagnetic wave, the electric field, the magnetic field and the direction of propagation are
options: E and B parallel, both perpendicular to the propagation
E perpendicular to B, both along the propagation
items.explanation: The three form a right-handed mutually perpendicular set, with propagation along $ \vec{E} \times \vec{B} $. Both fields being transverse is what makes electromagnetic waves polarizable, and it is why polaroid sunglasses work.

items.prompt: In an electromagnetic wave, the average energy density of the electric field compared with that of the magnetic field is
items.explanation: The two energy densities are $ \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E^{2} $ and $ \frac{B^{2}}{2\mu_0} $, and substituting $ B = E/c $ with $ c^{2} = 1/\mu_0\varepsilon_0 $ makes them identical. The energy is shared exactly equally between the electric and magnetic parts of the wave.

sections.title: The Spectrum and Radiation Pressure
sections.blurb: One family of waves, differing only in frequency.

items.prompt: Arranged in order of **increasing** wavelength, the correct sequence is
options: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible, X-rays, gamma rays
visible, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays, infrared, radio
gamma rays, X-rays, ultraviolet, visible, infrared, microwaves
microwaves, infrared, radio waves, visible, X-rays
items.explanation: Gamma rays have the shortest wavelengths (below $ 10^{-12} $ m) and radio waves the longest (metres to kilometres), with the visible band a narrow slice around $ 400$–$700 $ nm. All travel at $ c $ in vacuum and differ only in frequency — the divisions between them are historical, not physical.

items.prompt: Electromagnetic waves carry momentum, so light falling on a surface exerts a pressure. For a **perfectly absorbing** surface, that pressure is
items.explanation: An absorbed wave delivers its momentum $ U/c $ entirely, giving a pressure $ I/c $. A perfect *reflector* receives twice as much, $ 2I/c $, since the momentum is reversed rather than merely stopped — the same factor-of-two as a ball bouncing versus sticking.

items.prompt: An electromagnetic wave passes from vacuum into glass. What remains unchanged?
items.explanation: Frequency is fixed by the source and survives any change of medium. The speed drops to $ c/n $ and the wavelength shrinks in proportion. This is the same rule met in wave optics — and it is why a colour does not change on entering water.

worked_examples.label: Example 1 — Speed of light from μ₀ and ε₀
worked_examples.problem: Compute the speed of electromagnetic waves in vacuum from $ \mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} $ and $ \varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} $ SI.
worked_examples.solution:
$ c = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}} $

**Product first:**

$ \mu_0\varepsilon_0 = (4\pi \times 10^{-7})(8.85 \times 10^{-12}) = (1.257 \times 10^{-6})(8.85 \times 10^{-12}) $

$ = 1.112 \times 10^{-17} $

**Square root:**

$ \sqrt{1.112 \times 10^{-17}} = 3.335 \times 10^{-9} $

**Hence:**

$ c = \frac{1}{3.335 \times 10^{-9}} = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $

**Why this was one of the great moments in physics.** $ \mu_0 $ came from experiments on forces between currents and $ \varepsilon_0 $ from experiments on forces between charges — neither had anything to do with light. That their combination reproduced the measured speed of light told Maxwell that light *is* an electromagnetic wave.

**A note on the modern definitions.** Since $ c $ is now defined exactly and the ampere is fixed by the elementary charge, $ \varepsilon_0 $ is the measured quantity and this relation is a definition rather than a discovery. The physics is unchanged; only which quantity is primary has shifted.

worked_examples.label: Example 2 — Field amplitudes in a wave
worked_examples.problem: An electromagnetic wave has an electric field amplitude of $ 300\ \text{V m}^{-1} $. Find the magnetic field amplitude and the wave's intensity.
worked_examples.solution:
**Magnetic field amplitude:**

$ B_0 = \frac{E_0}{c} = \frac{300}{3 \times 10^{8}} = 1 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{T} $

Just one microtesla — some fifty times weaker than the earth's field.

**Intensity:**

$ I = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E_0^{2}c = \frac{1}{2}(8.85 \times 10^{-12})(9 \times 10^{4})(3 \times 10^{8}) $

$ = \frac{1}{2}(8.85 \times 10^{-12})(2.7 \times 10^{13}) = 119\ \text{W m}^{-2} $

**Why $ B_0 $ always looks so small.** Dividing by $ c $ makes the magnetic amplitude tiny in SI units — but this is a unit artefact, not a physical asymmetry. The two fields carry *equal* energy densities, as shown by substituting $ B = E/c $ into the two expressions.

**For a sense of scale:** sunlight at the earth's surface delivers about $ 1000\ \text{W m}^{-2} $, so this wave is roughly a tenth as intense — comparable to bright indoor lighting.

worked_examples.label: Example 3 — Displacement current in a charging capacitor
worked_examples.problem: A parallel-plate capacitor of area $ 100\ \text{cm}^{2} $ is charged so that the electric field between its plates grows at $ 10^{12}\ \text{V m}^{-1}\text{s}^{-1} $. Find the displacement current.
worked_examples.solution:
$ i_d = \varepsilon_0 A\frac{dE}{dt} $

$ = (8.85 \times 10^{-12})(100 \times 10^{-4})(10^{12}) $

$ = (8.85 \times 10^{-12})(10^{-2})(10^{12}) = 8.85 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{A} $

About $ 89 $ mA.

**Why Maxwell needed this term.** Apply Ampere's law to a loop encircling the wire feeding a capacitor. Choose a surface that cuts the wire and you enclose the conduction current; choose one that passes between the plates and you enclose *no* conduction current at all — yet the same loop cannot have two different answers. The displacement current between the plates resolves the contradiction, and it exactly equals the conduction current in the wire.

**What it is not.** No charge crosses the gap. It is a *changing electric field* that produces a magnetic field just as a real current would — which is precisely the effect the compass-in-the-gap question probes.

worked_examples.label: Example 4 — Energy density in an electromagnetic wave
worked_examples.problem: Sunlight at the earth's surface has intensity about $ 1000\ \text{W m}^{-2} $. Find the average energy density and the electric field amplitude.
worked_examples.solution:
**Energy density.** Intensity is energy density times speed:

$ u = \frac{I}{c} = \frac{1000}{3 \times 10^{8}} = 3.33 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{J m}^{-3} $

**Electric field amplitude.** From $ I = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon_0 E_0^{2}c $:

$ E_0 = \sqrt{\frac{2I}{\varepsilon_0 c}} = \sqrt{\frac{2000}{(8.85 \times 10^{-12})(3 \times 10^{8})}} $

$ = \sqrt{\frac{2000}{2.655 \times 10^{-3}}} = \sqrt{7.53 \times 10^{5}} = 868\ \text{V m}^{-1} $

**And the magnetic amplitude:** $ B_0 = E_0/c = 2.9\ \mu\text{T} $.

**Two things worth noticing.** The energy density of full sunlight is minute — a cubic metre of sunlit air holds only microjoules of radiant energy. Yet the field amplitude of $ 868\ \text{V m}^{-1} $ is substantial, comparable to the fields inside electronic components.

**Why solar panels need area.** With so little energy per cubic metre, capturing useful power requires intercepting a large cross-section — which is the fundamental reason solar farms occupy the space they do.

worked_examples.label: Example 5 — Radiation pressure
worked_examples.problem: Find the force sunlight exerts on a perfectly reflecting sail of area $ 100\ \text{m}^{2} $ held perpendicular to the beam, taking $ I = 1400\ \text{W m}^{-2} $.
worked_examples.solution:
**Radiation pressure on a perfect reflector:**

$ P = \frac{2I}{c} = \frac{2(1400)}{3 \times 10^{8}} = 9.33 \times 10^{-6}\ \text{Pa} $

**Force:**

$ F = PA = (9.33 \times 10^{-6})(100) = 9.33 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{N} $

Under a millinewton — about the weight of a tenth of a gram.

**Why the factor of two.** An absorbed photon delivers momentum $ p $; a reflected one delivers $ 2p $, since its momentum is reversed. Same reasoning as a ball bouncing off a wall versus sticking to it.

**Why solar sails still work.** The force is feeble but it never stops, and in space there is nothing to oppose it. Sustained over months, $ 10^{-3} $ N on a light craft produces a large velocity change — and it needs no propellant at all. Japan's IKAROS demonstrated this in 2010.

**Where radiation pressure genuinely dominates.** Inside stars, where it helps hold the star up against gravity, and in comet tails, which are pushed away from the sun by sunlight and the solar wind.

worked_examples.label: Example 6 — Wavelength across the spectrum
worked_examples.problem: Find the wavelength of (a) a $ 100 $ MHz FM radio wave, (b) a $ 2.45 $ GHz microwave and (c) an X-ray of frequency $ 3 \times 10^{18} $ Hz.
worked_examples.solution:
Use $ \lambda = c/\nu $ throughout.

**(a) FM radio:**

$ \lambda = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{10^{8}} = 3\ \text{m} $

**(b) Microwave oven:**

$ \lambda = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{2.45 \times 10^{9}} = 0.122\ \text{m} = 12.2\ \text{cm} $

**(c) X-ray:**

$ \lambda = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{3 \times 10^{18}} = 10^{-10}\ \text{m} $

**What each wavelength explains.** The three-metre FM wave needs an antenna of order a metre — hence the size of car aerials. The $ 12 $ cm microwave sets the scale of an oven cavity, and the standing-wave pattern inside it is why food must be rotated. The $ 10^{-10} $ m X-ray matches atomic spacings in crystals, which is exactly why X-ray diffraction reveals crystal structure.

**The unifying point.** All three are the same phenomenon, travelling at the same $ c $, differing only in frequency by ten orders of magnitude — and every practical difference between them follows from the wavelength.

worked_examples.label: Example 7 — Wave in a dielectric medium
worked_examples.problem: An electromagnetic wave of frequency $ 5 \times 10^{14} $ Hz travels through a medium of relative permittivity $ 2.25 $ and relative permeability $ 1 $. Find its speed, wavelength and refractive index.
worked_examples.solution:
**Speed in the medium:**

$ v = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}} = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\mu_r\varepsilon_r}} = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{\sqrt{1 \times 2.25}} = \frac{3 \times 10^{8}}{1.5} = 2 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m s}^{-1} $

**Refractive index:**

$ n = \frac{c}{v} = 1.5 $

**Wavelength in the medium.** The frequency is unchanged:

$ \lambda = \frac{v}{\nu} = \frac{2 \times 10^{8}}{5 \times 10^{14}} = 4 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m} = 400\ \text{nm} $

(In vacuum it would be $ 600 $ nm.)

**The relation worth carrying:** $ n = \sqrt{\mu_r\varepsilon_r} $, which for most transparent materials reduces to $ n = \sqrt{\varepsilon_r} $ since $ \mu_r \approx 1 $. Glass with $ \varepsilon_r = 2.25 $ has $ n = 1.5 $ — and this connects an *electrical* measurement to an *optical* one.

**A subtlety worth knowing.** The $ \varepsilon_r $ measured at low frequency often does not predict the optical $ n $, because $ \varepsilon_r $ itself varies with frequency. Water is the famous case: $ \varepsilon_r = 80 $ statically would predict $ n = 9 $, whereas the optical value is $ 1.33 $.

worked_examples.label: Example 8 — Photon count in a light beam
worked_examples.problem: A $ 10 $ mW laser emits light of wavelength $ 632.8 $ nm. How many photons does it emit per second? Take $ h = 6.63 \times 10^{-34} $ J s.
worked_examples.solution:
**Energy of one photon:**

$ E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{(6.63 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{632.8 \times 10^{-9}} $

$ = \frac{1.989 \times 10^{-25}}{6.328 \times 10^{-7}} = 3.14 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J} $

Or about $ 1.96 $ eV.

**Photons per second:**

$ n = \frac{P}{E} = \frac{0.010}{3.14 \times 10^{-19}} = 3.2 \times 10^{16}\ \text{s}^{-1} $

Thirty-two thousand million million photons every second.

**Why light normally looks continuous.** With $ 10^{16} $ photons per second arriving, the graininess is utterly invisible — the wave picture is an excellent description. Only at extremely low intensities, where individual photons arrive seconds apart, does the particle nature become directly observable.

**The bridge to the next chapter.** This calculation used $ E = hc/\lambda $ — a *particle* property — to describe a beam we have just been treating as a *wave*. Both descriptions are needed, and reconciling them is where the photoelectric effect leads.
